common_name: Darth Ciduous Daylily (Near-Black Eyezone Small-Flowered Daylily)

planting.note: Plant bare-root fans in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Darth Ciduous is a small-flowered diploid daylily bred by Scott Elliott with heavy branching and a high bud count that give it a long midseason bloom period once established.

directions: Bred by Scott Elliott, Darth Ciduous is a small-flowered diploid daylily bearing dark purple, nearly black blooms over a compact green throat that extends a short distance up the midribs, giving one of the darkest eyezones found on a small-flowered cultivar. Scapes run about 28 inches tall carrying roughly 3.25-inch flowers, with heavy branching and bud count that support a long midseason bloom with rebloom. It has placed repeatedly in regional daylily shows for best small flower, reflecting its clean, saturated color and strong garden performance. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep flowering vigorous.

common_name: Hat's Off to Sue Daylily (Giant Multicolor Red-Eyed Daylily)

planting.note: Plant bare-root fans in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Hat's Off to Sue is a semi-evergreen diploid daylily with an unusually large, multicolored eye and strong rebloom that benefits from a full season to establish before clumps reach peak bud count.

directions: Hybridized by Tim Herrington and registered in 2008, Hat's Off to Sue carries an exceptionally large eyezone for a 4-inch flower, a bold red eye edged in pink that spreads across most of the bloom above a green throat, with red, pink, yellow, green, and white all visible at once. Scapes reach about 25 inches on a semi-evergreen, fragrant, diploid clump that produces heavy bud counts and dependable rebloom through the season. It has been recognized within the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award program for outstanding eyed or banded daylilies, reflecting both the drama of its eyezone and its reliable garden performance. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Don C. Stevens Award

common_name: One Eye Willie Daylily (Lavender-Pink Purple-Eyed Daylily)

planting.note: Plant bare-root fans in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; One Eye Willie is a fragrant, semi-evergreen diploid daylily with heavy branching that blooms early and reliably reblooms later in the season.

directions: Hybridized by Tim Herrington and registered in 2006 from a cross of Green Rainbow and Baby Boomer, One Eye Willie bears lavender-pink, 4-inch flowers with a bold purple eye above a green throat on scapes about 28 inches tall. It is a fragrant, semi-evergreen diploid daylily with heavy branching and bud count that blooms in the early season and reblooms reliably as the season continues. The cultivar has received the American Hemerocallis Society's Award of Merit and its Annie T. Giles Award for outstanding small-flowered daylily. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain strong flowering.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Annie T. Giles Award

planting.note: Plant bare-root fans in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sun Panda is a semi-evergreen daylily with a high-contrast eyezone that blooms in the mid-to-late season.

directions: Hybridized by B. Culver and registered in 2009, Sun Panda bears brilliant yellow-gold, ruffled flowers about 5 inches across, each marked with a deep black-wine eyezone and a matching picotee edge above a green throat. Scapes reach roughly 35 inches on a semi-evergreen clump that blooms in the mid-to-late season, and the cultivar has drawn recognition within the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award program for outstanding eyed and banded daylilies. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep bloom production strong.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Don C. Stevens Award

common_name: Quasar Cutie Daylily (Lavender-Pink Blue-Eyed Small Daylily)

planting.note: Plant bare-root fans in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Quasar Cutie is a vigorous, slightly fragrant small-flowered daylily that reblooms readily through the season.

directions: Hybridized by Kathleen Ann Nordstrom from a cross of Little Leprechaun and Height of Fashion and registered in 2018, Quasar Cutie is a small-flowered diploid daylily with lavender-pink, 4-inch blooms marked by a lavender-blue eye and a yellow throat, with faint radiating midribs that give the eyezone a starburst pattern. Scapes stand about 34 inches tall on a vigorous clump that reblooms readily through the season. It has received the American Hemerocallis Society's Annie T. Giles Award for outstanding small-flowered daylily. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Annie T. Giles Award

common_name: Dietmar's Wisdom Daylily (Magenta-Red Purple-Banded Small Daylily)

planting.note: Plant bare-root fans in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Dietmar's Wisdom is a small-flowered evergreen diploid daylily with heavy budding and branching that give a long bloom period with rebloom.

directions: Hybridized by Dominique Elliott and registered in 2016, Dietmar's Wisdom is a small-flowered, evergreen diploid daylily bearing magenta-red, 3.25-inch blooms with a dark purple band above a green throat. Heavy budding and branching give scapes of about 24 inches a long midseason-to-late bloom period with reliable rebloom. It has received the American Hemerocallis Society's Annie T. Giles Award for outstanding small-flowered daylily and has repeatedly placed as best small flower in regional shows. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep flowering strong.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Annie T. Giles Award

common_name: Halloween Green Daylily (Orange Red-Eyed Daylily with Green Throat)

planting.note: Plant bare-root fans in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Halloween Green is a small-flowered, semi-evergreen daylily with heavy branching and bud count that blooms early-midseason with rebloom.

directions: Hybridized by Tim Herrington from a cross of Green Rainbow and Amazing Morris Kirby and registered in 2011, Halloween Green is a small-flowered, semi-evergreen daylily with orange, 3.5-inch blooms marked by a triangular red eye above an unusually large, intensely green throat. Scapes reach about 24 inches with heavy branching and bud count, blooming in the early-midseason with rebloom. It has received the American Hemerocallis Society's Annie T. Giles Award for outstanding small-flowered daylily, prized for the vivid orange-red-green combination that gives the cultivar its Halloween-themed name. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society — Annie T. Giles Award

common_name: Beauty of Richmond Clematis (Pale Lavender Large-Flowered Jackmanii-Group Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Beauty of Richmond is a vigorous Jackmanii-group clematis that flowers on both old and new wood, so light pruning after the first flush preserves the most bloom.

directions: Beauty of Richmond is a vigorous Jackmanii-group clematis bearing large, 6-to-8-inch, pale lavender-blue flowers with a deeper lavender bar down each tepal and dark anthers, opening in flushes in late spring to early summer and again in late summer to early fall. Give it roots that stay cool and shaded while the vine itself climbs into full sun to light shade on a sturdy trellis or obelisk, since it readily reaches 10 to 15 feet. Because it reblooms on both old and new wood, prune only lightly, removing dead or weak stems in late winter rather than cutting the whole vine back hard. Water regularly through the growing season and mulch to keep the root zone cool.

common_name: Victor Hugo Clematis (Deep Violet Non-Clinging Late Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Victor Hugo flowers on new growth, so cut the whole vine back hard to a low pair of buds each late winter along with other pruning-group-three clematis.

directions: Victor Hugo is a late large-flowered clematis with a non-clinging, sprawling habit, bearing small, deep violet, 3-inch flowers with darker violet-tipped anthers from early summer into fall. Because its grip is weaker than many large-flowered hybrids, it benefits from being tied in or woven through a wall shrub, trellis, or wire support rather than left to climb entirely on its own, and it reaches 8 to 10 feet over a season. It flowers on new growth, so cut the whole vine back hard to a strong pair of buds about 12 inches from the ground each late winter, the standard treatment for pruning-group-three clematis. Water regularly during the growing season and keep the root zone shaded and mulched.
sources: Clematis on the Web (University of Hull)

common_name: Bonne Esperance Dahlia (Dwarf Single Mignon Pink Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 3-4 inches deep after last frost; Bonne Esperance is a compact, free-flowering mignon dahlia suited to edging, window boxes, and containers rather than the back of the border.

directions: Introduced in 1948, Bonne Esperance is a dwarf single (mignon) dahlia that stays a compact 12 to 18 inches tall while covering itself with a profusion of small, roughly 1.5-inch, bright pink flowers with a vivid yellow center from midsummer into fall. Its low, tidy habit and heavy bloom count make it one of the most popular dahlias for edging, window boxes, and other containers where taller exhibition types would be out of scale. Pinch the growing tip when young to encourage branching and deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep the long flowering season going. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8, or treat as an annual.
sources: American Dahlia Society — Single Dahlia Classification

common_name: Penhill Dark Monarch Dahlia (Giant Informal Decorative Dinnerplate Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Penhill Dark Monarch produces some of the largest blooms of any commonly grown dahlia and needs staking early to support its tall stems and heavy flower heads.

directions: Penhill Dark Monarch is a giant informal decorative, dinnerplate-type dahlia with loose, ruffled blooms that regularly reach 10 to 12 inches across, their broad petals twisting and curling slightly at the tips for a softer, wind-tossed look rather than the tight symmetry of a formal decorative. Color blends smoky plum, dusty raspberry, soft apricot, and muted lilac tones across the petals, so individual blooms vary from darker and moodier to warmer and paler. Plants grow tall on strong, sturdy stems well suited for cutting, but the sheer size and weight of the flowers make early staking essential. It blooms from midsummer until the first frost; lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.
sources: American Dahlia Society — Giant Decorative Dahlia Classification

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Barbarry Ball is a vigorous, free-flowering ball dahlia valued for its perfectly rounded blooms and strong, straight stems that make it an excellent cut flower.

directions: Barbarry Ball is a classic ball-type dahlia bearing fully rounded, densely packed blooms in a strong orange, generally 4 to 6 inches across, held on strong, straight stems that have long made it a favorite cut flower. The plant is a vigorous grower that flowers heavily from midsummer to the first frost. Disbud side buds for larger, show-quality blooms, or leave them intact for a bushier plant with more numerous, slightly smaller flowers. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.
sources: American Dahlia Society — Ball Dahlia Classification

common_name: Blyton Softer Gleam Dahlia (Golden Apricot Ball Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Blyton Softer Gleam is an exceptionally prolific, weather-resistant ball dahlia with long, strong stems that make it a favorite among cut-flower growers.

directions: Blyton Softer Gleam is a ball-type dahlia whose round, fully double, roughly 5-inch blooms open a warm golden orange and gradually soften as the petals unfurl, finishing in a pale honey-apricot shade reminiscent of wheat straw brushed with color. It is an exceptionally prolific, weather-resistant bloomer with long, strong stems, qualities that have made it a favorite among cut-flower growers and florists. Plants grow to around 4 feet and benefit from early staking to keep the long stems upright under the weight of the blooms. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8.
sources: American Dahlia Society — Ball Dahlia Classification
